title: Four tests for binary informational substitutes
oneLine: For two yes-or-no signals, four exact inequalities decide whether every partial disclosure preserves a specified diminishing-returns property.
abstract: A candidate classification gives four necessary-and-sufficient weighted-square inequalities for a binary event and two binary signals under a quadratic score, using Chen–Waggoner March 2017 Definition 2.2.3. A conditional-variance identity and concavity reduce arbitrary measurable disclosures to two endpoints in each orientation, including zero-probability cells. Rational failures have explicit two-report witnesses. The package also gives an oriented finite-signal extension, strong-complements tests, and a reviewer-derived strict separation from projective substitutes.

keyResults: Four weighted-square inequalities are necessary and sufficient for Chen–Waggoner strong substitutes for binary E, A and B under the fixed quadratic score, including zero-support cases.
A failed rational-input inequality yields an explicit rational two-report disclosure and a directly checked negative score gap.
The conditional-variance argument extends in one direction to a binary source and finite second signal, including square-integrable targets.
Reviewer-derived Proposition 4 proves strong substitutes imply projective substitutes in this model, strictly; Appendix A gives endpoint/vertex tests for strong complements.
evidence: Written proof and precise source comparison; exact rational classifier and failure witnesses; finite algebraic, support and direct-score checks; separately implemented checker; optimized replay and semantic negative controls; review response, AI index and manifest.
statusDetail: Unrefereed candidate with a written universal proof and internally replayed exact finite checks. No external peer review, independent reproduction, formal verification or historical-priority proof is claimed. narration:
Suppose two forecasters each have a yes-or-no signal about the same yes-or-no event. Does learning more from one forecaster always reduce the extra value of hearing from the other?

That sounds like a simple question about diminishing returns. But checking only what happens when both signals are revealed completely can miss the answer. One forecaster might reveal a carefully chosen, randomised fragment of their information.

This Evidence Press candidate reduces that whole family of disclosure choices to four exact tests, for one specified quadratic scoring rule. There are two tests for each order of the signals. If all four pass, every admissible partial disclosure satisfies the stated diminishing-returns condition. If one fails and the probabilities are rational, the software constructs a concrete two-report disclosure that demonstrates the failure.

The proof turns the information problem into the shape of a curve. For each order, the relevant curve is concave. Its two endpoint values therefore decide whether it can dip below zero. This is an analytic argument, not a claim that a computer tried every possible disclosure.

The package includes the proof, exact checking software, thousands of finite test cases and explicit counterexamples. A comparison added during review shows that another condition, called projective substitutes, can hold even when this stronger condition fails.

The limits matter. The main classification is for two binary signals and a fixed score. It is not a general theorem about every forecasting system, and it does not test real-world forecast data. Internal checks are not independent external reproduction or formal verification.

The paper and evidence accompany Four tests for binary informational substitutes, released on the eighth of October twenty twenty-six. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional mathematical evidence.
